book_context: The plot runs on bluff, impersonation and withheld knowledge. Tuppence's 'Jane Finn' bluff, Tommy's bargain in Soho, and Jane's feigned amnesia all mirror Mr. Brown's own mask. Brown is the 'nonentity' with an ordinary face, hidden in a crowd. All through the book Sir James drops hints and Julius keeps secrets (the safe), so the reader is set to suspect each in turn. Chapters XXIV–XXVI hold the double reveal in strict order. XXIV: Julius rescues the girls, and Tommy turns the gun on him for reasons left unexplained. XXV: Jane's story, then Sir James accuses 'Julius.' XXVI: Sir James unmasks himself and dies. XXVII then explains everything at the Savoy, through Tommy's account and Brown's diary. Setups to keep intact: the 'Twopence' note, the Marguerite/Faust picture, the peep-hole, Little Willie, the brandy, the photograph in the safe, the recess curtain, the Argentine note, and Tommy's uncle and Tuppence's father.
continuity_checks: 'Little Willie' introduced before the countdown and the 'persuade' joke.
Whittington is named at the door, so the reader knows the butler of Chapter XXIII.
Tuppence learns Annette = Jane in the car, before Chapter XXV's train scene.
Tommy's motive is unexplained; there is no hint of Sir James's guilt.

essential: Kramenin at Claridge's is greedy for the millionaire and lets him in; Julius insists the secretary leave the suite entirely.
At gunpoint Julius sizes Kramenin up as an abject physical coward. Kramenin first denies knowing Jane Finn.
Kramenin fears Mr. Brown, has met him without knowing it, and could not recognise him again.
Julius argues that money will get him off as insane, so he will not hang; this convinces Kramenin, who is corrupt himself.
Location given: Astley Priors, Gatehouse, Kent. Kramenin says the girl has lost her memory and that the other girl is there too.
Julius takes Kramenin along so he cannot telephone his friends. The chauffeur George is hostile to Bolsheviks. The terrifying drive with tall tales leaves Kramenin as putty.
At the door Kramenin claims betrayal; Whittington checks 'orders--from him?' and hands over both cloaked girls.
Another man recognises Julius and shoots; Julius fires back and tells Tuppence that Tommy is off to the Argentine. Kramenin is released and flees.
Julius identifies 'Annette' as the real Jane Finn. An ambush follows and Julius's cheek is grazed. Jane drops her accent, admits the fake amnesia and weeps; Julius declares himself her cousin.
Tommy climbs over the back of the car and orders the girls onto the train to Sir James. He snatches Julius's revolver and threatens him. Tuppence trusts him: 'If Tommy’s sure--he’s sure.'
Do not explain Tommy's motive, and do not hint at who Brown is.

voice_profile: Brisk, light-comic thriller voice. Most of the story moves through quick dialogue, broken by dashes and suspense ellipses, with italics for emphasis. The narrator adds dry, ironic asides ("using the words that have created many unnecessary panics"; "Julius’s narrative style, if not strictly accurate, was picturesque!"). Each character has a strong verbal tag. Julius speaks in American slang and tall talk ("Little Willie," "Sure thing," "I guess"). Tuppence is pert and bossy. Tommy is curt and understated. Sir James speaks in measured, lawyerly cadence. Kramenin is shrill and hissing. Melodrama is played straight and then punctured by a joke.
